          Spain Built the Youth Development Pathway England Still Crave
        
      
                          
                      Sep 25, 2026
          
                      Ryan Benson / Author, Jakob Abrahamson / Design, Peter McKeever / Data Viz
                  
      
              
                      
                  
          

    
              
      
              
                    
Spain have won successive major international men's tournaments. The pathways from academy football to senior teams at La Liga clubs has undoubtedly helped.
Drastic, nationwide reviews of football development in specific countries are ordinarily associated with prolonged fallow periods or short spells of extreme underperformance.
Two relatively recent high-profile examples would be Germany and England.

For Germany, a disappointing quarter-final exit to Croatia at the 1998 World Cup proved a pivotal moment for a re-think and increased investment behind the scenes in youth football. So, when there was outrage and calls for root-and-branch investigations in the wake of the national team failing to get out of their group at Euro 2000, strides had actually already been made. Germany went on to finish as runners-up at the 2002 World Cup, third at both the 2006 and 2010 World Cups, before winning it in 2014.

England, meanwhile, failed to even qualify for Euro 2008, and that was followed by an exit to Germany in the last 16 of a thoroughly underwhelming 2010 World Cup campaign. About six months after the latter, the FA unveiled its Youth Development Review, which provided 25 recommendations intended to improve the standard of football at every level, but especially in the grassroots game.

This review is broadly accepted as being a major catalyst for England's significantly improved results at major men's international tournaments in recent times, with the Three Lions reaching as many semi-finals (4) across the World Cup and European Championship since 2018 as they had in their entire history before Russia 2018.
How does any of this relate to Spain, then?
Well, if you're looking for similarities with respect to underperformance, it doesn't really relate at all, and that's the point.

Over several years, Spain did their own review of youth development and is currently in the second phase of a 10-to-12-year La Liga-led National Plan for the Optimisation and Improvement of Youth Academies, essentially a strategy to professionalise them. But as Juan Florit, La Liga's head of football projects, explains, academy reform in Spain was different to the prior examples because it was not triggered by a crisis.

“Traditionally, when a country, an organisation such as La Liga or a football association begins such a project, you start it from a position of weakness, from a problem or from a negative situation,” he says when asked by Opta Analyst about the initiative's grounding. “But if we think that with this it will be enough for the first decade, sooner or later we will be behind other countries [again].”
In 2016, clubs from the top two divisions began hosting annual Youth Academy Meetings with the intention of sharing knowledge, methodology and tools, hoping to improve competitiveness.

Granted, at this point Spain had recently underwhelmed at Euro 2016, having also failed to impress at the 2014 World Cup. But still, this was only four years on from winning Euro 2012, their third successive triumph at a major international tournament. Spanish football was hardly in crisis.
The Youth Academy Meetings ultimately led to the 2022 creation of the aforementioned ‘National Plan', which set out to take “grassroots football to a new level”.

It comprised five key principles: infrastructure, resources and technology; comprehensive player care; development and transition to professional football; training model and transition to competition; and structure and professional development.

This wasn't a reaction to any extreme underperformance either. The senior side had got to the semis of the delayed Euro 2020 a year earlier and the final of the 2021 Nations League. And at youth level, their Under-19s and Under-17s had each reached at least the last four of their most recent respective Euros in 2019 (youth tournaments in 2020 and 2021 were cancelled due to the COVID-19 pandemic).

While the phrase “if it isn't broken, don't fix it” does spring to mind, Spanish clubs and authorities spotted an opportunity to help themselves. If all academies were more professionally run, every club could potentially stand to benefit. At the very least, the steady stream of domestic players coming through and supplying the national team would be maintained.
“We thought that we needed to do something,” says Florit. “Other countries like Germany, Austria and Sweden were starting good projects with a solid base and a long-term vision.
“[Before] there was no real collective plan, collective vision, or collective strategy to work within the academy system and to strengthen the development of young talents [across Spain].”

And while that may have been the case, the domestic contingent in La Liga was already very strong and remains as such, perhaps to a degree most won't be fully aware of. This is their position of strength.

For the 10 seasons prior to 2026-27, the average number of Spanish players to play more than 450 minutes (so, the equivalent of five full matches) in a campaign is 236.6, a figure that dwarfs the rest of the big five leagues. The next closest is Italians in Serie A (152.2), followed by French players in Ligue 1 (149.9), Germans in the Bundesliga (142.6) and then English players in the Premier League (117.7).
